title: Version a Policy Through a Change
scenario: It is 6:25 AM. The threshold policy is changing, and the decision arrived the way real decisions do: as an email chain where an early proposal was superseded. Your job is to record the CURRENT policy - at the right version, with a note explaining what changed and why.
input:
[Mon 4:12 PM] Risk Desk Lead -> Desk Manager:
Proposing we keep routine at 5% and escalation at 12% for next quarter.

[Mon 5:30 PM] Desk Manager -> Risk Desk Lead:
Too noisy last quarter - we escalated eight times and six were nothing. Raise both.

[Mon 6:02 PM] Risk Desk Lead -> Desk Manager:
Agreed. Routine moves to 6%, escalation to 14%, effective tomorrow. This supersedes my earlier proposal.

[Mon 6:05 PM] Desk Manager -> Risk Desk Lead:
Approved. Version it and note the reason.

The current policy on file is version 1.0.0 (routine 5, escalation 12).
instructions: Read the chain to its conclusion - the first proposal was superseded.
Record the NEW thresholds as plain numbers.
Bump the version: a threshold change on an existing 1.0.0 policy makes this 1.1.0.
Write a changeNote stating what changed and why.
Keep escalation greater than routine, then validate.
copilotPrompt: Record the final agreed policy from this email chain as JSON: policyName, version (bump 1.0.0 to 1.1.0 for a threshold change), owner, approver, routineThreshold and escalationThreshold as plain numbers (use the superseding values, not the first proposal), and a changeNote explaining what changed and why.
successMessage: Policy versioned through a change. Downstream steps now read the current rule, and the audit trail explains the old one.

intro.heading: Before you build: policies change; versions remember

sections.title: The superseded proposal trap
sections.body: The chain contains two sets of numbers. Automations that scrape the first match get yesterday's rule. Reading a decision thread to its CONCLUSION - and knowing what superseded what - is a real skill this lesson makes explicit.

sections.title: Version bumps carry meaning
sections.body: 1.0.0 to 1.1.0 says: same policy, changed values. The version is how Risk Evaluation can say 'I classified today under 1.1.0' - without it, historical decisions become unexplainable.

sections.title: The change note is the why
sections.body: Six of eight escalations were noise - THAT is why the thresholds moved. A policy that records why it changed can be challenged, defended, and changed again intelligently. One that does not just drifts.

intro.jsonExample:
{
  "policyName": "Outage Alert Policy",
  "version": "1.1.0",
  "owner": "Ops Lead",
  "approver": "Site Manager",
  "routineThreshold": 8,
  "escalationThreshold": 20,
  "changeNote": "Raised both bands; last quarter's alerts were mostly noise."
}

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: You'd write the threshold rules down in a shared doc or a config tab (e.g. 'flag if move > 8%') so the check reads one source of truth, not memory.

bestFit.how: an Environment Variable or a SharePoint config list read at run time, never a hardcoded number
Workflow Static Data or an environment variable holding the limits
load thresholds from a config file so changing them needs no code deploy

takeaway.heading: Policy versioned through change
points: You read a decision thread to its conclusion and recorded the superseding values, not the first match.
The version bump (1.1.0) makes every past and future classification explainable against the rule that was in force.
The changeNote preserves the reasoning - noisy escalations - so the next change starts from evidence, not folklore.
Risk Evaluation on this tier will classify against 6/14; watch how the same workflow behaves under a changed rule.
The workflow can now evolve its business rules without losing its history.
